planting.note: Direct sow in fall or late winter in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Alamo is a hybrid turnip greens variety bred for moderate bolt resistance and tolerance of aphids and mosaic virus, with vigorous regrowth for repeated cut-and-come-again harvest starting as early as 33 days.

directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Alamo is a modern hybrid turnip grown for its greens rather than its roots, producing up to 50% higher yield than standard turnip greens varieties along with excellent regrowth after cutting, letting a single planting support several harvests through the cool season. It shows moderate resistance to bolting and tolerates aphids and mosaic virus better than many older turnip greens varieties, useful for stretching a spring planting later into warming weather. Harvest young leaves at 6-10 inches for the most tender greens, cutting to about 4 inches above the crown and allowing regrowth for the next cutting. Because it establishes and regrows quickly, Alamo suits both a fall planting for winter greens and a spring planting for an early crop.
sources: seed catalog reference (Stokes Seeds, Park Seed, Gurney's)

planting.note: Direct sow in cool to moderately warm weather; succession sow every one to two weeks for continuous harvest. Sora is notably heat tolerant, holding round roots without becoming pithy or hollow even as soil warms toward summer, extending the Gulf South radish season past the point where most varieties fail.

directions: Sow seed directly half an inch deep and thin to about an inch apart for well-formed roots; Sora is a round red radish notable for holding good quality in warmer soil than most radish varieties tolerate well, resisting the pithy, hollow centers that quickly ruin radishes grown too far into rising spring heat. This heat tolerance makes it a useful choice for extending the Gulf South radish season later into spring or for an earlier-than-usual fall planting while soil is still warm. Keep soil evenly moist for the crispest texture, and harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch across, since even heat-tolerant radishes eventually turn woody if left too long.

planting.note: Direct sow in cool soil; Merlin carries intermediate resistance to downy mildew and Cercospora leaf spot along with high resistance to bolting, a strong disease package for the Gulf South's humid, changeable spring beet season.

directions: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Merlin is a hybrid beet bred with intermediate resistance to downy mildew and Cercospora leaf spot, two fungal diseases that can blemish and weaken beet tops in humid, wet conditions, along with high resistance to bolting even through a swing of cool-to-warm spring weather. It produces smooth, uniformly round, deep red roots with sweet, tender flesh and good, dark green tops usable as cooking greens. Thin seedlings to 3-4 inches apart for well-sized roots, keep soil consistently moist, and harvest once roots reach 1.5-2.5 inches across for the best texture and flavor.

planting.note: Direct sow in cool soil; Boro's foliage resists common foliar blights and the roots are very resistant to bolting with good shelf life after harvest, useful traits for an extended Gulf South beet harvest window.

directions: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Boro is a hybrid beet whose tops resist common foliar blights that can weaken plants in humid, wet weather, while the roots show strong resistance to bolting and hold good quality in storage after harvest longer than many varieties. It produces smooth, round, deep red roots with sweet, tender flesh and healthy dark green tops good for cooking greens. Thin seedlings to 3-4 inches apart for well-sized roots, keep soil consistently moist, and harvest once roots reach 1.5-2.5 inches across; Boro's good storage quality makes it a solid choice for gardeners who want to hold part of the crop rather than using it all immediately.

common_name: Diablo Brussels Sprout (Disease-Resistant Frost-Sweetened F1 Hybrid)

planting.note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost for a fall-into-winter crop; Diablo carries strong overall disease resistance including tolerance to white blister and ring spot, and sprouts sweeten with frost exposure, well suited to an extended Gulf Coast winter harvest.

directions: Start seeds indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into rich, firm, well-drained soil with consistent moisture; stake tall plants; when bottom sprouts reach marble size, remove the growing tip to concentrate the plant's energy into sprout development. Diablo is a hybrid Brussels sprout bred with strong overall disease resistance, including tolerance to white blister and ring spot, two fungal diseases that can disfigure sprouts in humid, wet conditions. Its sprouts sweeten after exposure to frost, so a Gulf Coast fall planting that carries into the region's cool but mild winter can produce a long, steadily improving harvest. Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward as they reach 1-1.5 inches across and are still tight and firm.

common_name: Hestia Brussels Sprout (AAS-Winning Heat and Cold-Tolerant Hybrid)

planting.note: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; Hestia is an All-America Selections Regional Winner for the Southeast, specifically validated for Gulf Coast-type climates, tolerating both warm weather during establishment and cool temperatures during sprout development, with sprouts resistant to bursting and rot.

directions: Start seeds indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into rich, firm, well-drained soil with consistent moisture; stake tall plants and top the growing tip once bottom sprouts reach marble size to concentrate the plant's energy into sprout development. Hestia was named an All-America Selections Regional Winner for the Southeast specifically for its ability to tolerate the warmer fall temperatures typical of a Gulf Coast growing season while still developing tight, high-quality sprouts as the weather cools, and its sprouts resist bursting and rot better than many older varieties in humid conditions. Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward as they reach 1-1.5 inches across and are still tight and firm, and expect flavor to sweeten after a light frost.
sources: All-America Selections — Hestia Brussels sprout Regional Winner
